paras: The shooting of Sam H. Hill took place near Arkansas City, Desha County, Arkansas, on August 19, 1910, when Deputy Sheriff J. P. Findley shot Hill, a Black man, after mistaking him for Henry Tucker, a fugitive wanted for the assault and murder of a white girl. The Associated Press reported Hill killed instantly, while a local dispatch described him as probably fatally wounded but still alive the next morning.

Desha County officers had been searching for three weeks for Tucker, wanted on a charge of criminal assault and the murder of a fourteen-year-old white girl, the daughter of William Brock. On the morning of August 19 the sheriff's office received word that Tucker could be found at a certain house in the country.

Findley slipped up to the house through the timber, dashed at a Black man sitting on the porch with his weapon ready, and called on him to throw up his hands. According to the Arkansas City dispatch, the man turned toward the house, and Findley, believing him to be Tucker running for a weapon, shot him through the body.

The wounded man proved to be Sam Hill, who was said to be under indictment for grand larceny and to have served a term in the Arkansas penitentiary. The dispatch stated that "No censure attaches" to the deputy's action, and no report of an inquest, of Hill's death, or of Tucker's capture appears in the coverage.

The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic gave the fullest account under the headline "Shoots a Man by Mistake," calling Tucker "a desperate character" and closing by clearing the deputy. Outside the state, the Montgomery Advertiser and the Pensacola Journal ran a brief Associated Press item from Little Rock on August 21, headed "Kills Wrong Negro" and "Wrong Negro Is Shot by a Deputy Sheriff." No Black-press report of the shooting was found.

The wire said Hill was "instantly killed," while the Arkansas City dispatch, written the next morning, reported him alive but not expected to live; the only account of why the deputy fired is his own.

reader.title: Shooting of Sam H. Hill
bases: A single deputy sheriff searching for a wanted man shot a Black man he mistook for the fugitive when the man ran from an order to surrender; no crowd or posse is reported (A1, A2, A3).

A local Arkansas City dispatch (A1) and the Associated Press wire from Little Rock (A2, A3) agree that Deputy Findley/Findlay shot Hill near Arkansas City after mistaking him for Henry Tucker, though they differ on whether Hill died.

accounts.label: Local dispatch (deputy's version)
accounts.gist: Findley crept up through the timber to a house where Tucker was reported to be, dashed at the man on the porch and called on him to throw up his hands; the man ran toward the house, and Findley, thinking Tucker was going for a weapon, shot him through the body. Hill was not dead the next morning but was not expected to live.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Findlay shot and killed Hill, whom he mistook for Tucker, after Hill started to run when ordered to surrender.

framing.detail: The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic headed it 'Shoots a Man by Mistake', stressed that Tucker was 'a desperate character', noted Hill was 'wanted also', and concluded that no censure attached to the deputy.
The Montgomery Advertiser ('Kills Wrong Negro') and the Pensacola Journal ('Wrong Negro Is Shot by a Deputy Sheriff') ran the brief AP item without comment.

versions.value: Shot and 'probably fatally wounded'; still alive the morning of Aug. 20

conflicts.note: The local Arkansas City dispatch is dated the morning after and reports Hill's condition directly, so it is the better evidence for his state on Aug. 20; no later report of his death or recovery was found.

conflicts.field: age of girl Tucker was accused of killing

sources.note: Local Arkansas City dispatch dated Aug. 20: Deputy Sheriff J. P. Findley shot Sam Hill, believing him to be Henry Tucker; Hill 'probably fatally wounded' and still alive that morning; 'No censure attaches' to the deputy.
quotes: Sam Hill, a negro, was shot and probably fatally wounded yesterday afternoon near this city by Deputy Sheriff J. P. Findley
This morning the negro is not dead, but his condition is serious, and it is believed that he cannot live.
No censure attaches to the action of the deputy sheriff in firing on the negro.
